lessons.title: Introduction to Capsule Making: Tools and Equipment
lessons.body: Capsule making turns moringa powder into easy-to-swallow doses. In Africa, where moringa is abundant, capsules let you sell a premium product with longer shelf life. To start, you need a few basic tools. A capsule filling machine is the biggest investment. Manual machines come in sizes: 100, 200, or 300 capsules per batch. A 100-capsule machine costs around $50-$100 and is perfect for beginners. You also need a tamper (often included) to compress powder, a capsule loading tray, and a scraping tool like a credit card or plastic spreader. For powder preparation, you need a fine sieve (60-80 mesh) to remove lumps, and a digital scale (0.1g accuracy) to measure powder and check capsule weight. A clean, dry workspace is critical. Moringa powder absorbs moisture, so work in a dry room. Wear gloves, a dust mask, and a hairnet to keep capsules clean. You'll also need empty capsules (size 0 or 00) and a drying tray or rack. For quality control, get a small brush to clean capsules and a moisture meter if possible. Start with a manual machine: it's affordable and teaches you the process. As you grow, upgrade to semi-automatic or automatic machines. Remember, hygiene is key: wash hands, sanitize surfaces, and keep powder sealed when not in use. With these tools, you can produce 100 capsules in about 30 minutes once you practice. This module will guide you step by step, from sourcing capsules to labeling your final product.

lessons.title: Sourcing Empty Capsules and Gelatin Alternatives
lessons.body: Empty capsules are the shell that holds your moringa powder. They come in sizes: 000 (largest), 00, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (smallest). Size 0 holds about 0.5 ml or 500 mg of moringa powder; size 00 holds about 0.7 ml or 700 mg. Most sellers use size 0 or 00. You can buy empty capsules from local pharmacy suppliers, online marketplaces like Jumia or Amazon, or directly from manufacturers in India or China. In Africa, check with herbal shops in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, or Accra. Prices vary: 1,000 empty gelatin capsules cost $10-$20. Gelatin capsules are made from animal collagen (usually pork or beef). For vegetarian or vegan markets, use HPMC (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) capsules, also called vegetarian capsules. They cost slightly more but are plant-based and appeal to health-conscious buyers. When sourcing, check quality: capsules should be clean, free of cracks, and fit together smoothly. Store them in an airtight container away from moisture and heat. Humidity can make capsules sticky or soft. If you live in a humid area, keep a desiccant packet with them. Also consider colored capsules: clear is cheapest, but colored (white, green) can hide powder color variations and look more professional. For small-scale production, buy in bulk to reduce cost. Always test a few capsules with your powder to ensure they fill well and don't break. If you plan to export, check regulations: some countries require specific labeling for gelatin source. For local sales, explain the difference between gelatin and vegetarian capsules to customers. This builds trust and may allow you to charge a premium for veggie caps.

lessons.title: Filling Capsules Manually and with Machines
lessons.body: Filling capsules manually is slow but possible for very small batches. You separate the capsule halves, fill the longer half with powder, and push the shorter half on. This method yields about 50 capsules per hour and is messy. A better manual method uses a capsule filling plate: a tray with holes that holds the capsule bodies upright. You spread powder over the plate, press it into the holes with a tamper, scrape off excess, then put the caps on. This can produce 100 capsules in 15-20 minutes. For larger scale, use a capsule filling machine. The most common is the manual capsule filler with a capacity of 100, 200, or 300 capsules. Here's how to use a 100-capsule machine: 1) Separate the machine into base, middle plate, and top plate. 2) Load empty capsules into the middle plateâbodies in the bottom, caps in the top. 3) Remove the top plate with caps and set aside. 4) Pour moringa powder onto the middle plate, spread with a scraper, and tamp down. Repeat until all holes are filled. 5) Place the top plate with caps back and press down to lock. 6) Remove the filled capsules. You can produce 100 capsules in about 10 minutes. For semi-automatic machines, you use a lever to tamp and eject, increasing speed to 300 capsules in 15 minutes. Key tips: Use finely sieved powder (no lumps) for even filling. Tamp gently but firmly to avoid breaking capsules. Check weight regularly: a size 0 capsule should weigh about 500 mg total (powder + shell). Adjust powder amount by tamping more or less. After filling, wipe capsules with a clean cloth to remove powder residue. Store in airtight containers. Practice with a few capsules first to avoid waste. With a manual machine, two people can produce 1,000 capsules in a day, which is enough to start a small business.

lessons.title: Making Moringa Tablets: Binding Agents and Pressing
lessons.body: Tablets are compressed moringa powder. They require a binding agent to hold the powder together. Common binders include microcrystalline cellulose (MCC), magnesium stearate (a lubricant), and sometimes starch or gum arabic. A simple recipe: 95% moringa powder, 3% MCC, 1% magnesium stearate, and 1% silicon dioxide (to prevent clumping). Mix thoroughly in a dry bowl. You need a tablet press. Manual single-punch presses cost $200-$500 and make one tablet at a time. Rotary presses are for large-scale production. For beginners, a manual press is fine. To make a tablet: 1) Weigh the powder mix for one tablet (e.g., 500 mg). 2) Pour into the die. 3) Pull the lever to compress. 4) Eject the tablet. It should be hard and not crumble. If it crumbles, increase pressure or add more binder. If it sticks, add a little more magnesium stearate. Tablets can be round, oval, or square. Size depends on die. A 500 mg tablet is about 10 mm diameter. After pressing, let tablets dry for 24 hours in a cool, dry place. Then test hardness: a simple test is to drop one from 30 cm onto a hard surface; it should not break. For quality, check weight variation: weigh 10 tablets, average should be within 5% of target. Tablets are popular because they are portable and have a long shelf life. However, moringa powder is sensitive to heat and pressure, so avoid excessive pressure that generates heat. Also, tablets may need a coating (like cellulose) to mask the taste and protect from moisture. Coating is optional for small-scale. Packaging: count tablets into bottles or blister packs. Label with dosage: typically 2-3 tablets daily. Always clean equipment after use to prevent contamination. With practice, you can make 100 tablets per hour with a manual press.

lessons.title: Quality Control for Capsules and Tablets
lessons.body: Quality control (QC) ensures your capsules and tablets are safe, effective, and consistent. Start with raw materials: moringa powder should be bright green, smell fresh, and be free of mold. Test moisture content: ideal is below 10%. You can use a moisture meter or oven-drying method. For capsules, check weight: weigh 10 capsules individually. The average weight should be within 5% of your target (e.g., 500 mg). Also check that capsules are not cracked or dented. For tablets, test hardness, friability (ability to withstand shaking), and disintegration time. A simple disintegration test: place a tablet in a glass of warm water; it should break apart within 30 minutes. If not, adjust binder or compression. Microbial testing is important if selling commercially. Send samples to a lab for total plate count, yeast, and mold. In Africa, many universities and private labs offer this for $20-$50 per sample. Also test for heavy metals if your moringa comes from polluted soil. For all products, keep records: batch number, date, weight, and any issues. This helps trace problems. Visual inspection: capsules should look uniform; tablets should have no cracks or chips. Packaging QC: check that labels are correct, bottles are sealed, and expiry dates are printed. Store products in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. For small-scale, you can do basic QC yourself: weight, appearance, and disintegration. For advanced, invest in a hardness tester ($200) and a friabilator ($300). Always maintain hygiene: clean equipment, wear gloves, and work in a dust-free area. If a batch fails, do not sell it. Instead, reprocess or discard. Consistent quality builds customer trust and allows you to charge higher prices.

lessons.title: Packaging and Labeling Capsules for Sale
lessons.body: Packaging protects your product and attracts buyers. For capsules, common options are plastic bottles, blister packs, and pouches. Plastic bottles with screw caps are cheapest and easy to fill. Use amber or opaque bottles to protect from light. A 60-capsule bottle is a standard size. For tablets, similar bottles or blister packs. Blister packs require a sealing machine ($100-$300) but look professional. For small-scale, start with bottles. Fill bottles in a clean area, using a funnel or counting tray. Include a desiccant packet to absorb moisture. Seal with a tamper-evident cap if possible. Labeling is crucial: include product name, ingredients, net weight, capsule/tablet count, dosage instructions, batch number, expiry date, and your contact details. In many African countries, you need a label with English and maybe local language. For export, follow destination country rules. Expiry date: typically 2 years from production if stored properly. Dosage: for moringa capsules, 2-3 capsules daily with meals. For tablets, 2-3 tablets daily. Add a caution: consult doctor if pregnant or on medication. Design: use a simple, clean label with a moringa leaf image. Print labels at a local print shop or use adhesive labels. Cost: 1000 labels cost $20-$50. Packaging cost per bottle: $0.20-$0.50. Selling price: a 60-capsule bottle can sell for $5-$10 locally, more online. For marketing, highlight health benefits: energy, immunity, nutrition. Sell at markets, health shops, and online. Always include your contact for repeat orders. Keep packaging hygienic: wash hands, use clean bottles, and avoid touching capsules. Proper packaging and labeling make your product look trustworthy and increase sales.

quiz.q: What is the typical capacity of a size 0 capsule?
quiz.explanation: Size 0 capsules hold approximately 500 mg of moringa powder.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to compress powder in a capsule filling machine?
quiz.explanation: A tamper compresses the powder into the capsule bodies.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of HPMC capsules over gelatin capsules?
quiz.explanation: HPMC capsules are plant-based and suitable for vegetarians and vegans.

quiz.q: How many capsules can a 100-capsule manual filling machine produce in about 10 minutes?
quiz.explanation: A 100-capsule machine fills 100 capsules in roughly 10 minutes.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common binding agent for moringa tablets?
quiz.explanation: Microcrystalline cellulose is a common binder in tablet making.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for moringa powder?
quiz.explanation: Moisture content should be below 10% to prevent mold and spoilage.

quiz.q: What does a disintegration test check for tablets?
options: C) How fast they break in water
quiz.explanation: Disintegration test measures how quickly a tablet breaks apart in liquid.

quiz.q: Why should you use amber or opaque bottles for packaging?
quiz.explanation: Amber bottles protect the product from light degradation.

quiz.q: What is the typical dosage for moringa capsules?
quiz.explanation: Common dosage is 2-3 capsules daily with meals.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a tool needed for capsule making?
quiz.explanation: An oven is not typically used in capsule making; it's for drying other things.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of magnesium stearate in tablet making?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium stearate prevents sticking by acting as a lubricant.

quiz.q: How can you test tablet hardness simply?
quiz.explanation: Dropping from 30 cm is a simple field test for hardness.

quiz.q: What should you do if a batch of capsules fails quality control?
quiz.explanation: Failed batches should not be sold; reprocess or discard to maintain safety.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of 1,000 empty gelatin capsules?
quiz.explanation: Empty capsules cost around $10-$20 per 1,000.

quiz.q: Which capsule size is the largest?
quiz.explanation: Size 000 is the largest capsule size.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a desiccant packet in packaging?
quiz.explanation: Desiccants absorb moisture to keep products dry.

quiz.q: How many capsules can two people produce in a day with a manual machine?
quiz.explanation: With practice, two people can produce about 1,000 capsules per day.

quiz.q: Which of these is a vegetarian capsule material?
quiz.explanation: HPMC (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) is plant-based.

quiz.q: What is the first step in using a capsule filling machine?
quiz.explanation: You first separate the machine into its plates to load capsules.

quiz.q: What is a common weight for a moringa tablet?
quiz.explanation: 500 mg is a typical tablet weight for moringa.

quiz.q: Which test is used to check tablet strength against shaking?
quiz.explanation: Friability measures resistance to abrasion or shaking.

quiz.q: What should be included on a product label?
quiz.explanation: Labels should include batch number, expiry date, and dosage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work in a dry room when making capsules?
options: B) To make capsules dissolve faster
quiz.explanation: Moisture can cause mold and make capsules sticky.

quiz.explanation: Manual tablet presses cost between $200 and $500.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a quality control check for capsules?
quiz.explanation: Taste is not a standard QC check; weight, appearance, and disintegration are.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sieve in capsule making?
quiz.explanation: A sieve removes lumps to ensure even filling.

quiz.explanation: Tablets should dry for 24 hours in a cool, dry place.
